(and perhaps the algebra hierarchy more generally).

There are two routes from Field to CommRing (that I know of), namely the lovely route docs#Field.toCommRing :

@[implicit_reducible, expose] def Field.toCommRing.{u} : {K : Type u} → [self : Field K] → CommRing K :=
fun K [self : Field K] ↦ self.1

and the scenic route, going through the instance docs#Field.toEuclideanDomain (which has had a reduced priority of 100 since the mathlib3 days https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib3/pull/1724 , when the typeclass inference algorithm was totally different, and which adds all sorts of other exotic fields like quotient and remainder as well as taking the instance apart to a certain extent), and then through docs#EuclideanDomain.toCommRing .

So which route is always taken by mathlib? Well of course typeclass inference doesn't care about the reduced priority instance Field.toEuclideanDomain when trying to solve CommRing R because that is not yet relevant. What is relevant is which of Field.toCommRing and EuclideanDomain.toCommRing is defined last, because both have default priority, and it happens to be EuclideanDomain.toCommRing, so we will always take the scenic route. Indeed I claim that setting the priority of Field.toEuclideanDomain to 100 may as well be a no-op (as would setting it to 9999), because there is only one instance whose conclusion is EuclideanDomain R and that's Field.toEuclideanDomain, so who cares what priority it has, it's going to be the only thing which is tried whatever the situation is.

Surely the correct approach to persuading typeclass inference to go via the direct route is to lower the priority of EuclideanDomain.toCommRing, simply on the basis that there are far far more results about fields than about Euclidean domains in mathlib, so probably it's worth trying fields first. I gave this a go in #39263 and it saves 500G instructions, giving speedups in totally random files like Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Adjoint and Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.RootSystem.GeckConstruction.Semisimple. It also speeds up FLT (which is of course the real reason I'm interested in this sort of thing).

I'm wondering whether it's worth trying to understand what has become of the algebra hierarchy more generally, and whether we have our priorities set correctly. The above story almost feels like a rookie error -- maybe it was right for Lean 3 but the prio 100 was ported to Lean 4 (and why not?) and in retrospect turns out to be a weird choice. How many other weird choices are there out there?
Can one instead increase the priority of Field.toCommRing? Or are there too many cases where we want to deduce CommRing from something else?

In any case, reducing the priority of EuclideanDomain.toCommRing makes a lot of sense to me.
The underlying issue is most likely also the cause for #min_imports showing files involving euclidean domains (or Lie algebras, for that matter) even though they are completely unnecessary.

Yeah that would also work and would probably have the same effect.

I agree that I have also seen many traces in ring/field theory which mention Lie algebras for no obvious reason at all and this would be another excellent place to look for this kind of shortcut.

Note also that this change does not "penalise files which are specifically about Euclidean domains" -- it is 100% green as far as radar is concerned. One would have to be more careful with Lie algebras because there is far more material about them.

That's a nice speedup. I'm not surprised that by choosing priorities you can get speedups, although in many other cases it's not so easy to know what instance should have the higher priority. Sometimes changing the priority is faster in one area, but slower in another.
In this case it's indeed pretty obvious.
Yes, maybe we can get ring theory a bit quicker and also completely screw up Lie algebras by tweaking some instance priorities (which of course would not be good)
I wonder if it'd be a good idea to fix "priority laundering", i.e. lower priority instances being chosen because they are required for a prioritized path.
Why is Lean obsessed with Euclidean domains? I remember this was happening also in the Lean 3 days. It is because it is the "last" instance that has been declared?

@Kevin Buzzard Did you try to run shake after reducing the priority? I bet you can remove a bunch of EuclideanDomain imports.

A more principled solution could be to replace docs#EuclideanDomain by a mix-in class IsEuclideanDomain, similar to the existing docs#IsDomain, docs#IsPrincipalIdealRing, docs#IsDedkindDomain etc. This would also make the hierarchy a bit more consistent. It would be interesting to compare the performance impacts.
The mixin wouldn't be a Prop-valued class, right? So Is... would be a bit misleading in the name.
Possibly EuclideanAlgorithm is a good name?

True. So maybe it would be

class EuclideanDomain (R : Type*) [CommRing R] [Nontrivial R] where ...

instead of

class EuclideanDomain (R : Type*) extends CommRing R, Nontrivial R where ...
I don't like EuclideanAlgorithm, because the algorithm is built on top of it. EuclideanDivision, perhaps?

I don't think there's any need to refactor EuclideanDomain. As Johan points out, it contains data (this is not a mathlibism, there is a norm function on a Euclidean domain) and it's not a preferred parent so it's always going to be complicated as far as typeclass inference is concerned; my PR just makes it less popular.

I merged master (with Kevin's change) into #39291 and benched it again. It gains another 137 G instructions, with apparently mostly positive effects, but also slow-downs in some files that appear completely unrelated (like Mathlib.Probability.Martingale.OptionalStopping), so there is likely some noise involved.

It is possible to make docs#IsEuclideanDomain a docs#Prop because there is a smallest Euclidean algorithm, so that being a euclidean domain (in a slightly generalized sense, but that should be OK in the usual sense too) is really a property. See that paper of Samuel, https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-8693(71)90110-4

Oh nice! The only reason I hesitate here is that there are (deep) questions about integers of number fields involving whether they are Euclidean with respect to the absolute value of the number field norm (and the relation of this idea to being Euclidean at all).

Looking at where EuclideanDomain is actually used in mathlib: seems that we have docs#EuclideanDomain.gcd which could as far as I can see be defined for principal ideal domains.

The other thing Euclidean domains have going for them is that they have a division: docs#EuclideanDomain.instDiv . This seems to be the main reason that they're used (e.g. this means that polynomials over a field have a division). But as David Ang pointed out to me last Thursday at Xena, all rings can now have a division as we have docs#IsDiscreteValuationRing.quotient , which was very surprising to me because three years ago we had a big discussion about this in #5930 and concluded that it was not a good idea.

Kevin Buzzard said:

all rings can now have a division as we have docs#IsDiscreteValuationRing.quotient

I don't understand its docstring btw. There's nothing about the euclidean algorithm in there?

docs#IsDiscreteValuationRing.quotient is defined noncomputably. Basically "if there exists a quotient, give me x/yx/yx/y, otherwise a junk value".

def quotient (x y : R) : R :=
  open Classical in if y = 0 then 0 else if h : y ∣ x then h.choose else 0

This is then used to define the EuclideanDomain structure on the discrete valuation ring,

def toEuclideanDomain : EuclideanDomain R where
  quotient := quotient
  -- the rest of the EuclideanDomain structure

Yaël Dillies said:

I don't understand its docstring btw. There's nothing about the euclidean algorithm in there?

Just go and read the definition, it's pretty clear what it's doing. And then read Oliver's objection here. But now we have it anyway.
But this definition only makes DVR an Euclidean domain. It does not make a general ring an Euclidean domain.
Yes but it's a division function on a general ring, not on a DVR.

The division function given for dvrs does not necessarily match the division function on a general euclidean domain. For example on the integers, the dvr function gives 3/2=0 while the euclidean division gives 3/2=1.
